title: Lives, labs and rights: how sudden aid cuts have shaken global health
label: 27 October 2026 · Global Health session
summary: Witnesses from community health groups, UNFPA, MSF and academic research described the rapid shock from large donor cuts—sudden service closures, lost data and jobs, rising risks to children and to infectious disease control—and debated what governments and donors should do next: safeguard core services, shore up local partners, protect diagnostics and surveillance, and press multilaterals to be accountable while not abandoning bilateral support.

chapters.title: Sudden cuts, sudden gaps
chapters.takeaway: Rapid donor funding withdrawals caused immediate service gaps, job losses and confusion for people who rely on HIV and reproductive health services.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We're hearing from frontline witnesses about big funding drops and the effects on global health—please introduce yourselves and say what you see on the ground.

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: I run a youth HIV support organisation in Nairobi. After the big US cuts, young people panicked—some texted me saying 'we're going to die'. Long-standing HIV services that had become trusted were suddenly disrupted.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Did you and the Kenyan Government know in advance about the cuts?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: No. I sat with Government on sustainability committees in 2024 but neither they nor we expected such an abrupt withdrawal. The system had to be integrated quickly and that caused chaos and people lost contact with care.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: In Zambia we lost scale at community level: Copper Rose used to reach 200,000 people a year; now it's about 45,000. About 84% of HIV funding in Zambia came from PEPFAR and much of SRH funding from the US and European donors—so cuts hit communities hard.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: In Ethiopia FGAE lost 40% of its budget in 2025. We lost 162 technical staff and withdrew from 366 public health facilities—people and outpatient follow-up vanished with the funding.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: Data access also collapsed: key health records and monitoring systems had been hosted on US government servers. When funding stopped, access to those systems was lost, undermining planning and trust.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You referred to deaths and projections—what did you mean?

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: A modelling study (Open Forum Infectious Diseases, 2025) that Ministry staff qualified estimated 32,000 preventable deaths in the first three months after the cuts; if disruption lasted four years it projected about 330,400 deaths. These are stark warnings.

chapters.title: Rights, politics and community services
chapters.takeaway: Political and ideological shifts—plus funding changes—have narrowed what can be said or funded, undermining sexual and reproductive health rights and services.

turns.speaker: Tracy Gilbert
turns.text: Have you seen ideological resistance to your work? What can the UK do to help?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: Yes. In Kenya a presidential remark stressing only 'male and female' stirred attacks on organisations serving queer people. Government restricted language—'rights' became politically sensitive—so services and CSE (comprehensive sexuality education) initiatives were curtailed.

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: In Zambia the word 'rights' was removed from Government SRH documents: 'SRHR' became 'SRH'. 'Gender' language was replaced with 'sex' in policy texts. Funding cuts forced civil society into survival fundraising, reducing advocacy capacity.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: We see foreign actors using funding and influence to shape policy; there's less transparency about MOUs and new drafts that emphasise family values. That coordinated push worries us and affects service provision.

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: UNFPA sees this as part political anxiety about demographics. Rights language is being contested in several countries. The UK, with diplomatic influence, can be a strong defender of SRHR and support accountability for multilateral funding.

turns.speaker: Tulip Siddiq
turns.text: So what practical steps do you want from the UK?

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: Reclaim 'rights' and 'choices' language, challenge misinformation with evidence, broaden coalitions beyond health, and make the human consequences of rollbacks and cuts visible to policymakers.

chapters.title: Research, labs and the threat of AMR
chapters.takeaway: Research and lab networks have been weakened by cuts, raising the risk of antimicrobial resistance and slower outbreak detection.

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: I study neglected bacterial infections. Sudden research funding stops meant trials and diagnostic work froze—patients in TB studies lost treatment paths and trust, increasing risks of onward transmission and drug resistance.

turns.speaker: David Taylor
turns.text: Can you give a concrete example?

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: My South African colleague Bavesh Kana saw NIH-funded TB trials stop; medicines were in freezers but staff couldn't administer them. He later found rising numbers of resistant TB strains among those cohorts.

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: Diagnostic capacity matters: an Ebola outbreak had a two-and-a-half-week delay in identification because the wrong species test was used—sequencing later confirmed Ebola. Weak labs and disrupted networks slow detection.

turns.speaker: Dr Kennedy Uadiale
turns.text: The Fleming Fund supported AMR labs; when that funding stopped some hospitals could not deliver lab results for months. For AMR we need continuous surveillance; abrupt funding stops break that chain and make policy-making harder.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: How should the UK help on AMR and diagnostics?

turns.speaker: Dr Kennedy Uadiale
turns.text: Champion rapid, affordable surveillance approaches, invest in laboratory networks and workforce, and support transitions so countries are not left with equipment but no staff or reagents.

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: Also protect institutions that set standards and provide reference materials—the UK has strengths here and if those capabilities recede it weakens global testing quality.

chapters.title: Responses, opportunities and what to protect next
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses urged protecting humanitarian and core SRH funding, supporting local partners, investing in data and workforce, and balancing multilateral and bilateral funding with accountability.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: Are there any opportunities from the funding shock?

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: Yes: use existing government systems instead of rebuilding, engage the private sector for commodities and services, invest in digital training to reduce repeated costs, and prioritise local organisations for sustainable delivery.

turns.speaker: David Mundell
turns.text: What could a Government do quickly to help sustainability?

turns.speaker: Dr Natasha Kaoma
turns.text: In Zambia I'd introduce small service fees and reform national health insurance to generate revenue, while protecting the poorest—this could help steady financing for services.

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: Kenya's wake-up is an opportunity: the state must prioritise health funding, properly resource social health insurance, and support community-based civil society which is the bridge to people, especially marginalised youth.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: Ethiopia is pushing domestic resource mobilisation and public-private partnerships, and has increased SRHR budgeting, but gaps remain. Civil society is expected to generate local income and cross-subsidise services.

turns.speaker: Dr Kirrily de Polnay
turns.text: MSF sees the worst cases when prevention and basic care are missing. We urge the UK to protect existing humanitarian and nutrition funds, keep accountability for multilateral spending, and ensure funds reach local actors.

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: UNFPA is focusing on local delivery—already delivering roughly 38% of funds via national partners and aiming for 45%—and on partnering with development banks to prioritise maternal health in big loans and investments.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: A final point from the Committee: investing only via multilaterals risks gaps. Should the UK spread its approach?

turns.speaker: Dr Jeanne Salje
turns.text: Yes for research partnerships: bilateral research funds like Newton and GCRF built scientist-to-scientist long-term links; without them, those vital collaborations and training pipelines weaken.

turns.speaker: Dr Kennedy Uadiale
turns.text: And multilaterals must be supported to maintain standards and technical guidance, but the UK should also keep direct support where that secures local labs, workforce and service continuity.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We heard about loss of services, threats to rights, and risks to disease control. We'll follow up on civil society impacts and accountability. Please pass our thanks to your teams.
